classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text:
Bonjour, everyone. Bonjour. A little French for afternoon. That's probably enough. Other than au revoir or something like that. Good French lesson for everyone.

So, we had a million takeaways last week, which is partially my fault, leading us to, I think we had five meditation break practices. Five different ones. Which is okay. We were all inspired by different things. But what we'll do in the meditation is we'll just try to focus on one thing. And it'll just be basically connecting to that thought: I really want to become someone who can make a difference.

Which is like we were talking a little bit in the class about growing our spiritual power as a Buddha. Which is a bodhisattva mind, a bodhichitta mind. So just really praying for that, wishing for that. I want to be someone who can really make a difference. That's my heart. So basically it'll just be a meditation on bodhichitta, but we'll kind of zoom in on that facet, that aspect of it.

classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text: I think that's it for me. We had the window open, that was helpful. But then our neighbors don't want to listen to our prayers too much. Okay, cool. Let's begin. Thank you.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy. May everyone be free from misery. May no one ever be separated from their happiness. May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such pure lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind teacher, source of all good; O bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just like the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara's ocean; O so that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common paths, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy teachers, O bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation on bodhichitta. By thinking: all living beings are drowning in the vast and deep ocean of samsara, taking rebirth after rebirth in boundless samsara. We can think: I cannot bear the suffering of these countless mother beings who have to experience various kinds of misery and pain in life after life without end. Through reflecting on this unbearable situation, we can think: at present I am unable to be of much help. Only a Buddha has sufficient spiritual power to really make a difference.

Just connect to this thought: I really want to make a difference, and therefore I will become enlightened. If this decision arises in our heart, we can just hold it single-pointedly. I will become enlightened for the benefit of others. I will develop this spiritual power so I can really make a difference. And if we lose it, then we can just go through the contemplation again.

Finally, we can ask ourselves: how will I put this into practice? What is my plan to really become someone who can make a difference, who can have sufficient spiritual power? Don't just have this be aspirational. Think it through. How can I put this into practice?

And then we can, in our own time, gradually arise from our practice.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
shantidevaReading.text:
All right, I'll do the reading for today. From Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. We're in a new chapter. Very thrilling. Purifying Negativity. It's page 15, or just Chapter 2, the first verse. So we'll do verses 1 through 18 today, and then we'll see what that looks like.

Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, Chapter 2: Purifying Negativity

(1) To maintain this precious mind of bodhichitta,
I make excellent offerings to the oceans of good qualities —
The Buddhas, the stainless jewel of the holy Dharma,
And the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(2) However many flowers and fruits there are,
And all the different types of medicine;
All the jewels there are in the world,
And all the pure, refreshing waters;

(3) Mountains of jewels, forest groves,
And quiet and joyful places;
Heavenly trees adorned with flowers,
And trees whose branches hang with delicious fruits;

(4) Scents that come from the celestial realms,
Incense, wish-granting trees and jewelled trees;
Harvests that need no cultivation,
And all ornaments that are suitable to be offered;

(5) Lakes and pools adorned with lotuses,
And the beautiful call of wild geese;
Everything that is unowned
Throughout all worlds as extensive as space —

(6) Holding these in my mind, I offer them well
To the supreme beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
O Compassionate Ones, holy objects of offering,
Think of me kindly and accept what I offer.

(7) Lacking merit, I am destitute
And have nothing else that I can offer;
Therefore, O Protectors, who think of the welfare of others,
Please accept these for my sake.

(8) Eternally I will offer all my bodies
To the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Out of respect, I will become your servant;
Please accept me, O Supreme Heroes.

(9) Being completely under your care,
I will benefit living beings with no fear of samsara.
I will purify my previous evils
And in future I will commit no more.

(10) Within this sweetly scented bathing chamber
With a clear and glistening crystal floor,
Majestic pillars ablaze with jewels,
And canopies of radiant pearls spread aloft;

(11) With many jewelled vases filled to the brim
With scented waters that steal the mind,
And to the accompaniment of music and song,
I offer ablution to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

(12) I dry their bodies with matchless cloths
That are immaculately clean and scented.
Then I offer to the holy beings
Fragrant garments in magnificent colours.

(13) With various excellent raiments, fine and smooth,
And a multitude of supreme ornaments,
I adorn Arya Samantabhadra,
Manjushri, Avalokiteshvara and all the others.

(14) Just like polishing pure, refined gold,
I anoint the radiant bodies of all the Able Ones
With supreme perfumes whose fragrance pervades
Every part of the three thousand worlds.

(15) To the Able Ones, the supreme objects of offering,
I offer all the beautiful, scented flowers —
Mandaras, upalas, lotuses and so forth —
And exquisite garlands, finely arranged.

(16) I offer them vast and fragrant clouds
Of supreme incense that steal the mind;
And I offer delicacies of the gods,
Together with a variety of food and drink.

(17) I also offer jewelled lamps
Arranged on golden lotuses;
And on polished ground sprinkled with scent
And scattered with beautiful flower petals,

(18) I offer to those with the nature of compassion
A celestial palace resounding with heavenly praise
And hung with beautiful pearls and jewelled ornaments
Whose infinite radiance illuminates space.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text:
Eureka! I was very pleased about the almost screaming in here. Everyone was really loud, except a few people who did nothing. So there were three people who were dead silent, and then they were screaming, which was great. I like the screaming. I don't like the nothing. But maybe you didn't have the book or something, which is okay. The idea is that we're all doing it together.

Because reciting the condensed meaning puts it on our mind and blesses our mind, and it's really, really important. In these verses, as we know, maybe the first eight are in Prayers for Peace. So when you do Prayers for Peace, you recite those eight verses. And then verses ten through thirteen or so are in the nunya practice. Some of them overtly, and some of them implied. And then the very famous and beloved nunya practice that we do on Buddha's Enlightenment Day. So these are very special verses that have been put into actual pujas, because they're so amazing and unique. So we want to recite them.

postMeditation.speaker: Sumit
postMeditation.text: If you want a job around that, please email me. This is Sumit.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text:
We'll talk about that a little bit more. It's 4 to 7:30. I'll say more about that later. It is part of the spiritual calendar. We have an aspiration to one day do it every month. We're not there yet, but we're moving in that direction. So it's nice to do it, since it landed on a TTP day.

Especially because we just had the Dorje Shugden empowerment. It's a great way — it's basically just a huge way to accumulate tons of merit, purify negativity, and receive blessings. So what a good thing to do, for three and a half hours.

Any data from the last week? We had all sorts of juicy nuggets going on. The cannibals practice, thinking, may I one day give you Dharma. A little bit about Lamrim, keeping Je Tsongkhapa at our heart all day. Thinking, I am making a difference, and I can make a difference, and so on, and other things. Okay, Anne, yes, thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text:
I've never done the Lamrim thing, where you go every 21 days around the world. I always kind of told myself, well, I'm teaching, so that's how I get my Lamrim in, because I'm teaching Lamrim pretty much. That's true, but I just never tried it. Suddenly, they were like, you should do it. So I did it. I just read a chapter in the Meditation Handbook, and did a little meditation on that every night before bed. It took me 15 minutes.

First of all, it just made me feel super solid. I'm doing it right. That was very satisfying and fulfilling for me, just that alone. But then I found each day, the first day afterward, all of a sudden, I had precious human life with me. Then the second day, I also had precious human life and death with me. Then the third day, I had precious human life and death with me. They were with me, like people reminding me all day long of all these things, and it didn't feel burdensome. It made everything very light, because I had all these friends reminding me of the correct view of everything, which is much lighter than the ordinary view of everything.

I had my usual worry about this or that, and I'm like, what about the hell realm? This is nothing. This is completely nothing. I'll finish with that. I'm really looking forward to the next seven days of this. This is awesome.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thanks, Anne. That was delightful. It's a nice point that you're mentioning about that it makes us feel very solid and grounded, but also light, and there's a lightness that comes from that grounding.

Many people's emotional problems just come because they don't actually meditate on the Lamrim. If they just meditated on the Lamrim, they wouldn't have those emotional problems. All the heaviness and intensity in people's lives is usually based on one-life thinking. If you just stop doing that, almost all of it goes away. That's like 99% of all the intensity and angst and worry. Just one-life thinking. Poof. Make that go away. We have a huge burden lifted, and then we become an actual Buddhist.

I'm not even really a Buddhist until then. Just a nice little role player, and then more and more and more, and then universal compassion and love and real renunciation and bodhichitta and emptiness. I'm just delighted. Thank you for sharing. Others? Fran, yes. Thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
I also took to heart what you said last week about that pretty much anybody you know that's made real progress spiritually does Heart Jewel and the Lamrim practice every day. I did Heart Jewel six out of seven days, which for me is tremendous because I've been not really doing much of a seated practice at all. I did also every day add a Lamrim meditation, and I did the reading in the Meditation Handbook.

This happened to me before when I've done the Lamrim with the handbook as opposed to my own interpretation, my own meditation of it. I realized that my object is slightly off, that what the meditations that I'm doing are more the analytic part, and that in the Meditation Handbook pretty much every meditation, the object is a determination. It's telling us what we need to do, not just how we need to feel or how to think, but how to get there.

Today when you asked us to think about our plan and how we're going to achieve the goal of bodhichitta, what came to mind was I don't have to figure that out. Je Tsongkhapa and Geshe-la have laid it all out for me. I really felt happy about this practice this week.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thanks so much, Fran. It's a really nice insight and a real object of rejoicing, I think. There's a reason the Lamrim is called The Stages of the Path to Enlightenment. That's their name, right? That's what Lamrim means. So it's like, do I want a plan on how to get enlightened? Hmm, what should be my plan? Probably the first thing I should check out is the thing called The Exact Way to Get Enlightened. That's what the name is. This is how you get enlightened. That's basically the name of it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
So you're right, Fran. It's natural that we would move towards that. And then your point about the object of meditation — yeah, that's very interesting. If we had more time and if we were feeling a little cheeky today, what we would do is we would go through each one and we'd quiz the whole room. What's the object of meditation for this? What's the object of meditation for that? I feel like we might be in the 20% category of accuracy in the room. As a general move. Not a criticism. Sometimes it's a little surprising.

Even like Precious Human Life — are we really clear? Often when I hear people teach on Precious Human Life, it's like, woo, my life! That's not the object of meditation. It's not woo. Or even death. Are we clear on the object of meditation? That's kind of two-ish. Are we clear on both of them? What they both are and the relationship between them?

So anyway, you're right. Our mind creates models of reality. It's never seen the truth. It's always just creating a model. All the time. Until we see emptiness directly. It will always be creating a model or an abstraction of what's there. Then it creates a model or an abstraction based on our own biases and preferences and what we like. It's very easy to do this with the Dharma. To just rely on our memory, our imperfect memory which is modeling what we want to be there or what we imperfectly recall is there. We're just relating to this very imperfect model.

Having something like the New Meditation Handbook and eventually memorizing verbatim important Dharma texts prevents this from happening where we have an imperfect model that we think is like the actual answer. It is really useful to actually have the physical thing there reminding us.

I have a friend who I've known for about 15-20 years, a Dharma practitioner. Every 2-3 years, he'll come up to me and he always goes through these cycles, but then every 2-3 years he'll be like, wow, I'm really excited! I'm doing the Lamrim again with the handbook! It's interesting. Every time he's really inspired, that's what he's doing. Then he'll get out of it and get into other things and other little Dharma pursuits. It's like clockwork. Then he'll come back to the handbook. He's like, I got the handbook with me! I'll see it in his bag. He's bringing it around with him like a handbook. In his hand.

That's just my agreeing with you, Fran, about that point. Thanks so much. I'm going to stop saying so much. I'd love to hear from some more people. David, yes?

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text: That was super helpful. Although it does raise a question for me because in Joyful Path, all the objects — like karma is however many pages, 70 pages on karma. This idea that the Lamrim object is a particular determination or two or something. I thought it was completely multifaceted and you could do a meditation and land on any aspect of the object? Or is it multiple objects? What's the right way to think about that?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
In each meditation there are many component parts and you can meditate on any of those individual component parts. But there's like a compound object of meditation. We could say it's like the main one.

Let's say I was going to make you an eggplant parmesan. Vegan eggplant parmesan. I could spend a lot of time learning how to make really good bread. That's one component. Then I could learn how to cut the eggplant just right and salt it just right to get the bitterness out. Then I could learn how to fry it just right and bread it just right. That's its own component part. I've got bread, I've got the eggplant, I've got the frying and the breading. Then I want to make a really good sauce. That's its own component part. I want to make a really good fake cheese thing. It's not too plasticky.

From one point of view I could just buy all that random stuff from the store and put it together, or I could learn over time how to make each part really well and put it together. With all the Lamrim meditations, the main object is marked in the New Meditation Handbook on how to understand the mind in the different Lamrim sections. The main object is very clear. That's like the eggplant parm. That's the main object.

If you study Joyful Path there will be parts that just say this is how you make the bread really, really good. This is how you make the sauce really, really well. We can zoom in on the component parts and do the Lamrim meditations, but we're never making the sauce for the sauce's sake. It's part of a whole. We always want to come back to the whole. That's the analogy that I find helpful.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
My data is about really stemming from what you said in the empowerment, one of the commentaries — Does What I Do Matter? Particularly just trying to have that thought throughout the day because I think in aggregate, intellectually I'd say yeah it matters, but really trying to zoom in moment by moment right now. Do I feel like this moment matters? Does this moment matter?

It's a little challenging actually. I find when I do the six sessions I can get there and I get a little experience of it and it helps a bit, and then it just dissipates. It's humbling to recognize how quickly my mind falls out of that.

Anyway it reminded me of what you said in class last week that I need more spiritual power. That's another aspect I've been trying to work on — just really working on concentration. Somehow I have this faith that if I can learn to concentrate for 30 seconds and then a minute and then 3 minutes and 5 minutes, like that power of my mind will sort of serve to bridge those gaps. I have some faith that over time eventually it will, but really trying to have a plan — the six sessions are good, but I'm not sure how to beef up the plan more than just really focusing on concentration.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, thanks so much, David. It's really nice data. These kind of situations are interesting because sometimes we have, for example, no six sessions, we have nothing to support our mindfulness, and then our mind goes a little wonky in little situations. And in those situations the idea is add more — add structures, add scaffolding, support it.

But then sometimes we add structures, we add some scaffolding and it still happens that our mind goes a little funny. And often in those situations the answer isn't add more, because we already have a good structure. We've already put a lot of time into the structure and maybe it's even a little bit of a push to have that structure. More might create a little bit of a burden or angst or just friction in our mind or tiredness.

In this case it does seem like you have all the right structures. And in those cases it's like, okay, then what's my takeaway when my mind goes a little funny? Is it the structures aren't working? No, I don't think so. Is it I have to add more? Nah, I don't think so.

Sometimes the takeaway is just: yep, it just takes time to reverse my karma — which is a very unglamorous answer but that's actually just often the answer. When we have a really good setup, when we're doing everything just right, it doesn't mean that our karma is going to instantly be reformatted. We're just still going to get weird minds, distracted minds, angry minds, ignorant minds, craving minds. This is normal. So sometimes it's just: okay, I'll just be patient with myself and keep up my structure.

Over-correcting in our Dharma practice can be a really bad habit. We try to create a structure that's based on our karma and our life and what we do, but then once it feels pretty good, we do try to let that ride a bit and not over-correct in either way and give it a little bit of space. If we over-correct then we end up kind of keep tearing things down that we set up and then we never build the deep habits that can last us decades — ones that are just fused in our mind. And that's what we really want.

Thanks so much. Okay, time for maybe one more person. Jose, yes, thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Jose
practiceReports.text:
The past few months I had to do some changes to my practice, changes in my schedule. I did switch from meditating every morning for a very long time to kind of splitting that through the day. At the beginning that worked very beautifully — I was meditating in the subway and the way to work and then the way back. It was working pretty well.

But then eventually the quality of my meditation started going lower and lower and lower until I got to a point where they completely disappeared. That had not happened for years. I had been meditating daily for maybe three years, and the bottom was two weeks — the week of the empowerment, actually, that week I didn't meditate at all.

So after the empowerment I decided just to completely restart again from zero, forget about the previous structure that didn't really work, and I just focused on: before leaving my home I'm going to meditate. I don't know if it's going to be 5 minutes, 10 or 30 minutes, but I'm just going to do it. And I did, and I've been doing that for the last two weeks, and it just comes back so fast. It's amazing how it feels when you are back to it and it's working well, and you see how all the different structures that I used to have start coming back pretty easily. That's been such a nice thing to experience.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thank you so much, Jose. It's lovely to hear. You built up that structure. It was a multi-year long structure that you chiseled into your mind. And so then you did switch it up a little bit and then you noticed the gradual decline — but fortunately the karma was in there. The grooves were cut into the mind to such a degree that they were still there even after that, and you could just hop back in there, get back into the swing of things.

Those changes can happen a bit subtly, and it's nice to catch them earlier than later. This is how it goes always. It's a reverse kind of hockey stick — it looks subtle going down, but that subtle is implying actually something that involves a free fall, vertical descent. And it's not a normal undulation in the practice. There's normal ups and downs and those are just normal.

But there's other ones that we start to notice over time — that this is like a pattern. This isn't a normal oscillation. This is momentum building in an unhelpful direction. And as you said, it's really good to go through it, and usually we go through it a few times in our practice. We find ourselves down here, usually hurting, and then we really eventually build up a skill that prevents that from happening, and we learn about the cues.

practiceReports.speaker: Kristin
practiceReports.text:
I just wanted to report in that I have been really enjoying doing the — you know, may I benefit this person with pure Dharma. A lot actually during work. I'll have moments that I'm sort of working with someone and we'll be doing something for a period of time, and it was a nice natural direction that my mind was drifting frequently, which was really nice to tie it in that way.

I've also been putting effort into Lamrim, revisiting the Lamrim this week with a different object every day. I'm just curious because I have been doing Blissful Path consistently every day basically since we studied that book, but it doesn't have Lamrim in it. I didn't know if there was a way to sort of build that in, or if I should just do as I have been, or as Anne did, to kind of just read a little bit and do a little meditation on Lamrim at a different time of day.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, great question, Kristin. It just depends on your schedule and what will work. If it feels too much of a push to kind of put it in there, then maybe just a little reading and reflection at night is great. You can just do it in bed even.

If it feels like, okay, I want to put it into the practice, then you can just do it after generating bodhichitta. Or like what I'll do sometimes is — if I'm on meditations one to six, I'll do it with the refuge part. And then if I'm on seven to 21, I'll do it with the bodhichitta part, because it kind of will feed. One through renunciation will feed refuge, and then seven through 21 will feed the bodhichitta. So you can just plug it in there if you'd like.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
All right, we are on to Disclosure of Evil. Best name of any chapter in any book. Again, more evil talk. Bring back evil. That's what I want.

Disclosure of Evil, page 59. The first chapter of his Guide, Shantideva discusses the benefits of developing the mind of bodhichitta. In the second chapter, he shows us how we can eliminate obstacles that would normally prevent us from developing this enlightened motive. Thus the outline of the commentary continues as follows: How to practice the six perfections once bodhichitta has been developed. This is two parts. Maintaining bodhichitta. How to practice the six perfections.

Maintaining bodhichitta — this section of the outline is two parts, corresponding to the second and third chapters of this commentary. How to destroy obstacles and purify evil. How to accept and hold on to the actual bodhichitta.

How to destroy obstacles and purify evil. As stated before, the main obstacle to developing bodhichitta is our accumulation of negative energy or non-virtue. If we want to develop beneficial states of mind, such as bodhichitta, we have to purify this non-virtue and replace it with virtuous or meritorious energy. This dual process of accumulating merit and cleansing ourself of non-virtue, or evil, is accomplished by performing the following preliminary practices and confession. The preliminary limbs of practice. The confession of non-virtue.

The preliminary limbs of practice — this is three parts. Offering, prostration, going for refuge. First preliminary limb: the practice consists of making offerings. Shantideva's discussion of this practice has two parts. The necessity of making offerings, recognizing the objects of offering. The actual offering.

In the second chapter, Shantideva is personally taking the part of someone who wishes to purify himself of accumulated non-virtue. He realizes the necessity of following the preliminary practices and declares it openly as follows: In order to maintain and complete the precious bodhichitta, the source of happiness for all universal beings, I will now make offerings to the objects of devotion — on the Tathagatas, those who have gone to suchness, the Buddhas, the jewel of holy Dharma, and those sons of Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, such as youthful Manjughosha, Avalokiteshvara, and others who possess oceans of excellence.

The actual offering — Shantideva now begins an exhaustive list of the various types of offering that can be presented to these three sublime objects: Buddha, Dharma, Sangha. These types of offering are divided into three parts. Unowned offering. Offering our own body. Mentally transformed offerings.

Unowned offering: All the following I offer up to you — whatever flowers there are, those that are most beautiful, fruits, medicinal herbs, numerous jewels, and pure, refreshing waters. Mountains of jewels, beautiful forest groves, and quiet and joyful places. Heavenly trees with the most beautifully blossoming flowers, and trees whose branches bow down with the weight of good fruit. Exquisite scents from celestial realms, incense wish-granting trees and jeweled trees, harvests that need no cultivation, and all ornaments worthy of offering. Lakes and pools adorned with magnificent lotuses and resounding with the beautiful sound of wild geese.

From the depths of my heart I offer up all these unowned gifts. From the limitless spheres of space, together with all that is worthy of offering, to the supreme beings, the Buddhas and their sons. Oh, compassionate ones, think kindly of me and accept these offerings of mine. I have little merit and no other gifts of beauty or value to offer. By your power, oh protectors, you who are concerned with all others, please accept these offerings for my sake.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Okay, so that's unowned offerings, which just means you're offering things you don't own. You just go to Prospect Park, you see a beautiful tree, you offer that to Buddha. Here, you enjoy. You hear some beautiful sound, good, you offer that to Buddha. You see a sunset, you just offer that to Buddha. So you're just taking unowned things and you're giving that to Buddha. You just do this all day. All beautiful things.

So then we have a big job in the second class, where we're going to use this as a little bit of a theme as we go through the Disclosure of Evil chapter, which is basically to try to understand our desire and our attachment better. It's nice — we just ended the last chapter getting this excitement for Lamrim. And as we might know, the three scopes of the Lamrim oppose three types of attachment.

The first scope of the Lamrim, meditations 1 through 5, oppose attachment to happiness in this life. The sixth meditation, renunciation, opposes attachment to future lives — happiness in future lives. Or just having happiness in samsara, happiness while grasping at a self. And then the great scope, meditations 7 through 21, opposes attachment to attaining spiritual realizations for our self, or attaining enlightenment for our self.

So there are different types of attachment, different levels of attachment, that are being opposed by all three scopes. So our Lamrim practice can help a lot reducing our attachment.

Buddha's teachings on how to work with attachment and overcome it are very unique. And many people who even study Buddhism get it very wrong through settling for something that's a bit ascetic or indulgent. Both of which are wrong, completely. It's because they lack an understanding of emptiness, which cuts us through either of these extremes. Being indulgent, which is like looking for happiness outside of ourself and objects of attachment. Or ascetic, which is like abandoning objects of desire externally while still harboring attachment in our heart. They're both insufficient tools.

So it would be really nice as a TTP for us to become very skilled at cutting through desires of attachment. Which, from one point of view, really involves understanding our desire. Why do we desire the things that we desire? What does it mean to really desire something for us?

Because Kadampa Buddhism is the union of sutra and tantra, we have to also investigate what's the role of our tantric practice in overcoming our attachment. A lot of it has to do with learning how to make offerings to the self-generation. When people get highest yoga tantra empowerment, there are various vows that are given, and one of them is: enjoy objects of desire as offerings to the self-generation. Not avoid, but enjoy objects of desire. It's a vow. It's one of the very few things you explicitly vow to do.

So we can think: what does it mean to promise to enjoy objects of desire as offerings to the self-generation? What's our relationship to our objects of desire? Is it mostly just avoidance, or is it indulgence? Those are those two extremes. And what's it like to find the middle way there?

Okay, so we're going to be looking at this in the next session, but maybe in the break we can all think about: what do we desire? What does it mean to really follow a desire for us? What's our relationship to things that are pleasurable for us right now? Is it healthy? Is it unhealthy? Is it balanced and sensible?

session1.dedication: Through the virtues we've collected, through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay, so now we'll look at this in a bit more detail about desire. So maybe the scope of this class can be just a little bit by way of introduction, and understanding our relationship to desire — both uncontrolled desires, a.k.a. attachment, and just desire in general, which is just wishing for things. That isn't a problem, right? We have to wish for enlightenment, we have to wish to benefit others. So desire in itself is definitely not a problem.

Desire 101. Aspiration, desire, wish — they're all synonymous. There's virtuous desires, and neutral desires, and non-virtuous desires, like wanting to harm someone. Wishing to become enlightened — virtuous desire. Wishing to benefit others — virtuous desire.

So desire by no means is the enemy. Attachment is the enemy. But pleasure is not the enemy, or pleasurable feelings are not the enemy. Attachment is. Attachment, as we know, is identifying a contaminated object, viewing it as a source of happiness, and then wishing for it. That's after ignorance, enemy number one.

As we know in sutra, the principal way that we cultivate non-attachment, or renunciation, is that we think about the faults of attachment, we think about the faults of samsara, and then we realize that we need to look for happiness from within, and ultimately realize emptiness, through practicing the three higher trainings. That's basically what the Four Noble Truths is about.

That's quite effective, and in very pure times, people can basically do that alone. Some people can in this world, too, but it's tricky, because the attachment of the beings in this world is so strong. That's why people live in monasteries — there's less things to get attached to.

Of course, we want to practice the pure sutra of renunciation. We do Lamrim meditation — the first five meditations, plus the renunciation meditation. They're all working towards building us that sutra of renunciation. In addition, with certain objects of desire, sometimes we create a buffer with them. That buffer might look like asceticism, but it's not exactly, because the intention is to create space so that we can actually transform our mind.

So in a moment, we're going to be looking at how to transform objects of desire through the tantric teachings. But it's not saying, don't use sutra of renunciation. That's a big part of it. And it doesn't mean don't have healthy boundaries around certain things. But just do it with the right motivation. The right motivation is so that I can transform my mind — not: this is my end goal, which is like I'm pushing things away.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Buddha taught how to transform our enjoyments into the spiritual path in the tantric teachings. And he taught that specifically for people with strong desires and attachment — the people of this world. But one thing we want to do is just try to understand our own desire a little bit.

You don't have to say it out loud, but just think to yourself: are you really in tune with what you desire right now? Not like what you're supposed to desire, not what you would tell a potential spouse or your sangha friends maybe, or your employer. But in the sort of raw space of your mind.

Some people just, if you ask them, what do you really crave? They're like, I'm not actually sure, because I'm so focused on what I'm supposed to do that they get a little disconnected. Some people who are spiritually minded can have this problem, because they practice a form of asceticism which is having that desire but then not following it, so much that that little voice of what we desire is muted. It's still totally as strong as ever. It's just not as clear.

The way you know that is if someone has rules about what they do and don't do, they relax the rule and then instantly go off the deep end. Detachment didn't even reduce much. It was simply held back by the rule.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Ultimately, we want to reach a place where our desires are all virtuous, right? But we love to do them as much as we would love to do anything else that we currently really love to do and look forward to.

So then, this practice of transforming enjoyments. Geshe-la says here, page 182, New Guide to Dakini Land, Making Offerings to the Self-Generation: Geshe-la gave many explanations showing the importance of making offerings to the self-generation and cited tantras to support his reasoning. In the root tantra of Heruka, Vajradhara says: Making offerings to our self becomes an offering to all Buddhas.

This is because when we absorb the wisdom beings, all the Buddhas dissolved into and merged inseparably with our self, generated as Vajrayogini. Moreover, during the practice of bringing death into the path to the truth body, we dissolved all environments and beings, including all Buddhas, into the clear light and identified this clear light as the truth body, which is one with the mind of all Buddhas. From this clear light, we arose in the form of Vajrayogini. Therefore, the self-generation is the synthesis of all Buddhas.

Making offerings to our self, generated as the deity, is an especially powerful method for accumulating merit. If we maintain the awareness, then whatever we enjoy, such as food and drink, becomes an offering to the deity. It is only in secret mantra that we have the opportunity to create merit in this way. If we fail to make offerings to the self-generation, the power of our tantric practice will diminish.

The complete purity of enjoyments is the viewing of every enjoyment as an offering to the self-generation. If we omit these offerings to the self-generation, our practice will not have the fourth complete purity. So it will not be a qualified tantric practice.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: What does self-generation mean? And what does deity mean?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, we'll get to all that.

Modern Buddhism, Preciousness of Tantra: Practicing sutra teachings is the basic foundation for practicing tantric teachings. And the practice of tantra is a quick method to fulfill the ultimate goal of sutra teachings. In his sutra teachings, Buddha encourages us to abandon attachment. In tantra, he encourages us to transform our attachment into the spiritual path.

Some people may think this is a contradiction, but it's not, because Buddha's tantric instructions on how to transform attachment fulfill the aims of sutra teachings. Attachment itself cannot be transformed directly into the spiritual path. It is a delusion, an inner poison, and an object to be abandoned in both sutra and tantra. So transforming attachment into the path means that we transform the causes of attachment — our experience of worldly pleasure — into the spiritual path.

So what we're looking at here is how do we transform experiencing worldly pleasure, which in and of itself is no problem — it's just pleasure, there's nothing wrong with that. There are different levels of doing this. And they're all related to where happiness is coming from.

Level one: just simply starting to see that our inner peace, our happiness, is within the mind. That's the beginning of the spectrum. Level two: finding pleasure and bliss from our love and compassion. It's like learning to find happiness and even bliss from our love and our compassion. Not from other people — from our love for them. Encapsulated in this little mantra: Other people can't make me happy, but my love for them can.

The bliss principally comes from recognizing this is coming from within. It's only when we really see that we're blissful because we think, wow, my mind is generating the entirety of this feeling. I don't need anyone or anything for this. This is entirely coming from within.

Level three: offering enjoyments, or the pleasure of enjoying any object of desire, to Buddha at our heart. Walk around all day with Je Tsongkhapa or Buddha at our heart and we just enjoy a coffee, a drink, a snack, a rest, a sunset, whatever, a beautiful song. We experience pleasure and we offer that to Buddha at our heart.

Level four: offering it to ourself as the self-generation, as the deity. What this means is thinking I on a Buddha's body and mind. Normally we think I on our ordinary body and mind. In self-generation we're thinking I on that Buddha. And because in the practice we develop the recognition that they're the synthesis of all Buddhas — then when we enjoy some pleasurable thing and offer it to the self-generation, we're making an offering to all the Buddhas.

This is a very clever practice. It does like a million things in one practice. Most simply, it turns the thing that binds us into samsara into an offering to countless Buddhas. You simultaneously subtract the cause of binding ourselves to samsara, but you simultaneously add an offering to all Buddhas. A million-for-one deal. Cutting the object that binds us to samsara and creating a ton of merit and good fortune. In addition, we deepen our self-generation practice. In addition, we are actually able to be in modern life and busy life without fear of increasing our delusions. It allows us to really be a modern Buddhist and really help people.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: Obviously Geshe-la talks a lot about real cause of happiness and changing sufferings. When I hear pleasure, to me included in that is these changing sufferings — not real happiness. Yes, I'm bought in on real happiness comes from within. But I do feel like I experience pleasure, changing-suffering types of pleasure, from without.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. Even from without, it's still coming from within, that pleasure in the mind. Even with changing suffering, it's still coming from within. You're right — the aim of this practice is definitely not to just have lots of changing suffering. We're not trying to have mind-blowing amounts of worldly pleasure. But part of the problem with changing suffering is that we're associating where the good feeling is coming from to the object.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: My understanding of changing suffering is that the reason it is pleasurable is that it's relatively better — like a good bagel versus a bad bagel. So it is coming from the bagel because this was the good bagel. Do you mean it just in the sense that everything we have, all of our experiences are mental in nature? Because it does seem like there is something like the good versus bad bagel.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, but that's just a view. That's still coming from within. Good bagel, bad bagel — it's still a view.

Let's take being full as an example. Some people hate feeling full. And some people eat three times after they're full. It's not enough to feel full — they want to feel really full. So where's the changing suffering coming from? It's not coming from the food. It's coming from some mental thing that's being escaped from. It's coming from a view.

Pleasant feeling is just coming from our karma that's ripening. As we know from How to Understand the Mind, the mental factor feeling is just how our karma ripens. And feeling only ripens in the mind. It doesn't come from objects.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: So would you say, just to follow up on Sumit's question, that changing suffering is like a pleasurable feeling plus this view that that's coming from the thing — like that's what makes it changing suffering? And we can take that pleasurable feeling and use it in some other way to not make it changing suffering?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah. Whenever we're experiencing some kind of changing suffering, we're still viewing it as coming from without. If we're 100% viewing the pleasure we're having as coming from within the mind, we're basically meditating on emptiness. Which is very pleasurable, but that's not changing suffering. That's meditating on emptiness as a virtuous object.

Coming from the mind, merely imputed, empty — are all synonyms. So if you have a pleasurable feeling and you're viewing it as merely imputed, you're saying this is empty. That is a beautiful, virtuous mind that's leading us out of samsara. There's not even pervasive suffering there. We've gone even deeper than just solving the changing suffering problem. We're marching out of here.

Just the simple exercise is very useful. As long as we're doing this to try to understand emptiness to some degree. We're taking some kind of pleasurable thing and trying to really see: this is merely imputed, this is just coming from mind, just empty. The more we stay with that, it will break down our attachment, but it will also be leading us out of samsara.

Sometimes when people look at this practice, they say, just enjoy the good feeling, but not with the object. But that's not exactly right. If you eat that cake, you get a good feeling, and then you just enjoy that good feeling, but if you don't make some emptiness connection, that's just enjoying a worldly pleasure. That's just changing suffering. That's not Buddhism.

It's only when we think, this is merely imputed, or this is coming from the mind — that's when it becomes a Buddhist teaching. We have to very consciously make that recognition.

teaching.speaker: Anne
teaching.text: Is it correct to say that what is really happening is that karma is ripening, we're experiencing pleasure, and then our ordinary mind generates an experience of something appearing outside of us to sort of generate or explain that good feeling?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, I think that's often what happens, yes.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: I'm confused. You dropped this big topic of desires, attachment, and then there's the sutra, and the tantra, and the different things all the way to self-generation. What am I supposed to do this week in particular? There's like 10 things you just put in 15 minutes.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Let's make it practical. Your question about how to practice — that's for your discussion partner.

Continuing — this is one thing that we want to do, related to seeing things as empty. Part of this practice too is we're just seeing: the thing that I find pleasurable is a creation of my mind. So I'm attracted to a creation of my mind. This is very similar to the Chittamatra view, that everything is the nature of the mind. But it's a very effective thing to meditate on.

We just take whatever we're attracted to and whatever we find pleasurable. And we're trying to meditate on this idea: I'm attracted to my own mind's creation. That is a very delightful and hilarious thing to meditate on. Wow, I'm really into my own creation. My own little fantasy object.

So this is very nice to meditate on also. And this is also helping us transform enjoyments. It's relating to the emptiness of things — here we're relating to the fact that it's empty because it's created by mind in general.

Actually offering to the self-generation or to Buddha at your heart: you just take something, you enjoy it. If you want to bless it first, you can recite Om Ah Hum three times and imagine it turns into nectar. Then you take the pleasure that's being experienced, and we offer it to either Buddha at our heart or self as a Buddha. Offering just means that which delights the Buddhas. We just delight in that pleasure as an offering.

Once we get some kind of blissful feeling, even just some pleasurable feeling, then we move into maintaining emptiness. Whatever rudimentary understanding we have. Even if it's just a space-like vacuity. We just feel: I'm meditating with a very blissful feeling on this space-like vacuity. And that's the part where the practice really becomes unbelievable, because it's the blissful mind that mixes with emptiness the best.

In sutra we develop the bodhichitta mind because that's the best sutra mind that mixes with emptiness. But in tantra it's the blissful mind that mixes best with emptiness. So whenever we get that good feeling, that blissful feeling, even if it's really not much, then we just do a little meditation on emptiness. Even if it's one second. The more we do this the more we realize: ah, every time I meditate on emptiness this is how I want to do it. It's much more profound. And it really starts to take us somewhere deeper.

So Ryan, you're lucky I can answer your question now. How can we all personally take this forward? That first bit with those million questions around desire is just one practice: understand our desire better. All those questions are facets of that one inquiry. Two, we can start working on any of these four points in this trajectory. Finding happiness from within in general. Finding happiness from our love, but making sure we're making the point this is coming from my mind, not from outside. And then offering to Buddha at our heart, offering to self-generation. You can't do all four in a week. Maybe just one.

And if you're going to get into especially the latter two, we're just trying to get into some emptiness understandings. We're trying to mix emptiness with this practice or else it doesn't work properly. Either by acknowledging the good feeling is coming from within, or just thinking: the thing I find attractive is just a creation of my mind. I'm attracted to a creation of my mind. I made something and then I got into it. I created a fantasy and then I got attached to my fantasy.

I remember early on in my practice, I was absolutely wracked with attachment and dissatisfaction. And I had a little talk with my teacher at the time. He asked me a handful of probing questions and then he just said: Ah, it's fine. Just take little, small pleasures and offer them to the guru at your heart or yourself as a self-generation. Just like a little cup of tea, he said. And basically that alone solved the problem. And it seemed so dumb. Like, that's the answer to my angst and my confusion? He was like, yeah, I'm really glad. I thought that would help. That just always stuck with me. These kind of things can seem like small things but they're really not. It's actually undoing our samsara from the inside through not running away from the things that we find pleasurable, but understanding our psychology with respect to them and then creating boatloads of merit on top.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Okay. We're out of time but I think it's clear what to do over the break. Do one of those things that we talked about.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
So we have two weeks. Do two of those things. Or one of those things for two weeks. Melodious Drum next week. That is our TTP class. It's not like TTP is off and there happens to be Melodious Drum. It's TTP equals Melodious Drum.

In the Melodious Drum practice we start with the praise to Manjushri. Then we do the Heart Jewel practice. Then we self-generate as Heruka. And then you do the whole practice as Heruka. Heruka's mandala is a blissful bonanza — not other than emptiness. You do the whole practice like that. It's three hours and 15 minutes of meditation as Heruka. Very blissful and delightful. You make millions of offerings to Dorje Shugden, but you're Heruka the whole time. And all the offerings are incredibly blissful — like yellow swans, and black dogs that roam like bears, and bone palaces. It just gets us all excited.

So let's please enjoy, and we can bring in a lot of what we looked at today into that practice. I think that's it for me. Thank you all so much. Thank you, online folk.

I'll just guide us with a little dedication here. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind. Enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. Thank you.

For those who kind of got some Lamrim stuff going on, please don't think what we looked at today is outside of that at all. The whole of the Lamrim is to take us into our heart. The whole thing is taking us into our heart. And those first two points on that spectrum, leading us to making offerings to the self-generation, are done by the Lamrim. It's not outside. It's not separate at all.

So please don't think in a chunky way — in a kind of bifurcated or siloed way — the Dharma. Don't think it's like we checked a box. Lamrim! Poof! On to this. It's not like that at all. Lamrim is like the basket that holds everything. This is just like one of the many jewels in that little Lamrim basket. So please don't think of this in a separate way.
